summary: Dynamic memory allocation lets a C program ask the runtime for a block of bytes while it is running, use it through a pointer, and give it back when finished. It exists because many sizes (how many records a file holds, how long a line is) are unknown at compile time and because some data must outlive the function that created it. The four tools are `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc` and `free` from `<stdlib.h>`, and almost every linked list, tree, hash table and growable buffer in C is built on them. Getting them wrong produces leaks, dangling pointers and heap corruption, which is why this topic is a staple of C interviews.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Variables you declare normally live in fixed-size storage: globals exist for the whole run and locals vanish when their function returns. Neither helps when you read an unknown number of items, or when a function must hand a freshly built object back to its caller. Dynamic allocation fills that gap. You request `n` bytes, the C library finds a block of that size in the **heap**, and returns its address as a `void *`. You own that block until you pass the same address to `free`.
bullets: **What you get**: a contiguous block of bytes, suitably aligned for any standard type, living until you free it.
**What you must do**: check for `NULL`, use only the bytes you asked for, free exactly once, and never touch the block afterwards.
**Where it sits**: the heap segment of the process, managed by the allocator in libc (glibc ptmalloc, musl, jemalloc and so on), not by the compiler.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
bullets: **Heap**: the region of process memory used for dynamic allocation; it is separate from the call stack and from static data.

**`void *`**: the generic pointer type returned by the allocators. In C it converts to any object pointer type implicitly, so no cast is needed (and a cast can hide a missing `#include <stdlib.h>` on old compilers).
**`malloc(size)`**: reserves `size` bytes. Contents are indeterminate (whatever was there before). Returns `NULL` on failure.
**`calloc(count, size)`**: reserves `count * size` bytes and sets every byte to zero. It also checks that the multiplication does not overflow and returns `NULL` if it would.
**`realloc(ptr, new_size)`**: resizes a block, keeping the old contents up to the smaller of the two sizes. It may extend in place or move the data to a new address.
**`free(ptr)`**: returns a block to the allocator. `free(NULL)` is defined to do nothing.
**Lifetime**: allocated storage lasts from the successful allocation call until `free`, independent of any function or scope.
**Ownership**: the part of the program responsible for calling `free`. Decide it for every allocation and document it.
**Allocation failure**: returning `NULL` when no block can be provided. On Linux with overcommit this is rare for small requests, but huge sizes and embedded targets do fail.
**Heap metadata**: bookkeeping bytes (usually the block size and flags) stored just before each block, which is why writing past a block can crash a later `free`.

sections.heading: How It Works
sections.body: The normal life cycle has four steps: allocate, check, use, release. The program below reads a count, allocates that many ints, fills them and frees them.
bullets: Write `p = malloc(n * sizeof *p)` rather than `sizeof(int)`: the size follows the pointer's type automatically.

`calloc(5, sizeof(int))` gives five zeroed ints; reading them is well defined for integers. All-bits-zero is not guaranteed to be a null pointer or 0.0 on exotic platforms, though it is on every mainstream one.
The block you receive is aligned for the strictest standard type, typically 16 bytes on 64-bit Linux, so you can store a `double` or `long double` in it safely.
After `free(p)` the pointer value is indeterminate. Setting it to `NULL` turns a later accidental `free(p)` into a harmless no-op and a later dereference into a clean crash.

sections.heading: Variants & Types
bullets: **malloc**: fastest, no initialization. Use when you will overwrite every byte anyway.
**calloc**: zeroed memory and overflow-checked size. Use for counters, flag arrays, and structs whose unset fields must be 0 or NULL.
**realloc**: grow or shrink. Use for dynamic arrays and string builders; always through a temporary pointer.
**free**: only for pointers returned by these functions, passed unchanged. Never for stack arrays, string literals, or pointers into the middle of a block.
**aligned_alloc (C11)**: block with a stricter alignment than normal, for SIMD or cache-line alignment; the size should be a multiple of the alignment.
**posix_memalign / mmap**: POSIX alternatives. `mmap` hands out whole pages straight from the kernel and is what malloc itself uses for very large requests (128 KiB by default in glibc).
**alloca / variable length arrays**: stack allocation, not heap. Fast, but no failure signal and a stack overflow if the size is large.
**Arena (region) allocators**: one big `malloc` carved up by a bump pointer and freed all at once. Excellent for parsers and per-request data.

sections.heading: Complexity & Costs
bullets: **Time**: a typical allocator serves small blocks from per-size free lists in tens of nanoseconds, but the worst case can involve searching or asking the kernel (`brk`/`mmap`), costing microseconds. Compare with a stack allocation, which is one subtraction.
**Space overhead**: glibc adds 8 bytes of header per block on 64-bit and rounds the total up to a multiple of 16, with a minimum chunk of 32 bytes. Allocating 1 byte therefore consumes 32 bytes.

**Growth strategy**: growing a dynamic array by a constant increment makes `n` appends cost O(n^2) total; doubling the capacity makes appends amortized O(1) at the price of up to 50 percent unused space.
**Fragmentation**: external (free space split into pieces too small for a request) and internal (rounding waste). Long running servers with mixed sizes are most affected.
**Cache behaviour**: nodes allocated one at a time can land far apart, so pointer-chasing structures are slower than arrays even with equal big-O.
**Thread contention**: a global allocator lock can serialize threads; modern allocators use per-thread arenas or caches to avoid this.

sections.heading: Common Pitfalls & Gotchas
bullets: **Memory leak**: losing the last pointer to a block, or returning early without freeing. The program keeps growing until the OS kills it.
**Use after free**: dereferencing a freed pointer. It often appears to work until the allocator reuses the block, then corrupts unrelated data.
**Double free**: freeing the same block twice corrupts allocator lists and is a classic exploit primitive. glibc aborts with `free(): double free detected`.
**Invalid free**: freeing a stack address, a global, a literal, or `p + 1` is undefined behaviour.
**Unchecked NULL**: dereferencing the result of a failed allocation.
**`p = realloc(p, n)`**: if it fails you overwrite your only pointer with `NULL` and leak the old block. Use a temporary.
**Wrong size**: `malloc(sizeof p)` allocates the size of the pointer (8 bytes), not the object. `malloc(strlen(s))` forgets the terminating NUL.
**Overflow in the size**: `malloc(n * sizeof(int))` can wrap for huge `n`, giving a tiny block that is then overrun. Use `calloc(n, sizeof(int))` or check `n > SIZE_MAX / sizeof(int)` first.
**Assuming zeroed memory**: `malloc` contents are garbage; reading them before writing is undefined behaviour for most types.
**Pointer invalidated by realloc**: any other pointer into the old block (an iterator, a `char *end`) dangles after a move.
**Zero-size requests**: `malloc(0)` may return `NULL` or a unique pointer that must still be freed; do not treat `NULL` there as failure without thinking.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
bullets: **Containers**: vectors, hash tables, linked lists, trees, graphs, and LRU caches all allocate nodes or backing arrays on the heap.
**Strings and buffers**: reading lines of unknown length (`getline` uses `realloc` internally), building output with growing buffers.
**Libraries and objects**: opaque handles such as `FILE *` or `sqlite3 *` are heap objects created by an `open` function and released by a `close` function.
**Kernel and embedded**: the Linux kernel uses `kmalloc`/`kfree` and slab caches with the same discipline; embedded systems often ban dynamic allocation after startup or use fixed pools.
**Tooling**: Valgrind, AddressSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address`) and `mtrace` find leaks and misuse; production servers swap in jemalloc or tcmalloc for lower fragmentation.

sections.heading: Interview Notes
bullets: **malloc vs calloc?** calloc zeroes the memory and takes a count and an element size (with overflow checking); malloc does neither.
**What does realloc return on failure?** NULL, and the original block is still valid and still yours to free.
**Does free(NULL) crash?** No, it does nothing.
**Why not cast malloc's result in C?** It is unnecessary, and in old code it could silence the warning for a missing `stdlib.h`. In C++ you must cast.
**How does free know the size?** The allocator stores metadata beside the block, which is why you pass only the pointer.
**Is the heap the same as the heap data structure?** No. Same word, unrelated concepts.
**How do you find a leak?** Run under Valgrind or build with ASan/LeakSanitizer; both report the allocation stack of unreleased blocks.

subtopics.title: malloc and the size expression
subtopics.summary: Request bytes, get an uninitialized block.

sections.body: `malloc(size)` takes a byte count of type `size_t`. The idiom `malloc(n * sizeof *p)` ties the size to the pointer type. For a struct, `sizeof *node` includes padding, so it is always right. For strings add one byte for the terminator.

`calloc(count, size)` multiplies for you and fails cleanly on overflow. Newly obtained pages from the kernel are already zero, so a good allocator can skip the memset for large blocks and calloc is then nearly free. Use it for tables where zero means empty, such as a frequency array or a hash table's bucket heads.

subtopics.title: realloc and the safe-resize idiom
subtopics.summary: Grow or shrink without losing the block on failure.

sections.body: If the new size is larger, the extra bytes are uninitialized. The block may move, so every old pointer into it is invalid afterwards. `realloc(NULL, n)` behaves like `malloc(n)`. `realloc(p, 0)` is not portable (implementation-defined, deprecated in C23), so call `free` instead. Always assign through a temporary.

subtopics.title: free and pointer hygiene
subtopics.summary: Release once, then forget the pointer.

sections.body: `free` does not change your pointer variable; it only tells the allocator the block is reusable. The usual defence is to null the pointer straight after. A helper macro keeps this consistent, but remember it cannot protect other copies of the same pointer, so single ownership matters more than the macro.

subtopics.title: Growable arrays
subtopics.summary: Doubling capacity gives amortized O(1) append.

sections.body: Keep a struct with data pointer, length and capacity. When the length reaches the capacity, double it. Total copying across `n` appends is at most 2n element moves, so each append costs O(1) amortized. Growing by a fixed step instead degrades to O(n^2).
Free with one call on `v->data`. If you keep pointers to elements, they dangle after a push; store indexes instead.
A contiguous block is fastest and needs one free. An array of row pointers allows ragged rows but costs `rows + 1` allocations and frees.
Prefer the contiguous or pointer-to-array form for numeric work: better cache use, one allocation, one free.

subtopics.title: How the allocator works
subtopics.summary: Free lists, bins, brk and mmap.

sections.body: A glibc-style allocator keeps freed chunks in bins grouped by size. A request first checks the matching bin, then splits a bigger free chunk, and finally extends the heap with `brk`/`sbrk` (the program break moves up). Requests above a threshold (128 KiB by default) are served by `mmap` and returned to the kernel with `munmap` on free. Adjacent free chunks are coalesced to fight fragmentation. Each chunk carries a size header; freed chunks reuse their payload to store list pointers, which is why use-after-free corrupts the allocator itself.
bullets: **Small block**: size class, per-thread cache, nanoseconds.
**Large block**: separate mapping, page-granular, costs a system call.
**Top of heap**: shrinking is only possible if the end of the heap is free, so a single live block can pin lots of memory.

sections.body: Standard allocators return memory aligned for `max_align_t` (16 bytes on x86-64). For 64-byte cache lines or 4096-byte pages use `aligned_alloc(64, size)` where size is a multiple of 64. Pool allocators carve equal-size slots from one block and keep a free list, giving O(1) alloc and free with zero per-object header. Arenas hand out memory by bumping a pointer and release everything with one `free`, ideal when many small objects share one lifetime.

subtopics.title: Debugging heap bugs
subtopics.summary: Tools that catch leaks and corruption.

sections.body: Compile with `-g -fsanitize=address,undefined` and run: ASan reports heap overflow, use-after-free and double free with the allocation and free stack traces, and LeakSanitizer lists leaks at exit. Valgrind needs no recompile (`valgrind --leak-check=full ./a.out`) but is slower. glibc can also abort on corruption (`MALLOC_CHECK_=3`). When a crash appears inside `free` or `malloc`, suspect a buffer overrun elsewhere that trashed the metadata.
bullets: `==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free`: touched a freed block.
`definitely lost`: no pointer to the block remains.
`Invalid write of size 4`: overran the block by one element or more.

takeaways: `malloc` returns uninitialized bytes, `calloc` returns zeroed bytes with overflow-checked sizing, `realloc` resizes, `free` releases.
Always check for `NULL`, write `p = malloc(n * sizeof *p)`, and free each block exactly once.
Resize with a temporary: `tmp = realloc(p, n); if (tmp) p = tmp;` so a failure does not leak the old block.
Doubling capacity makes growable-array append amortized O(1); fixed increments make it O(n^2) overall.
The three heap bugs are leak, use-after-free and double free; ASan and Valgrind find all three.
The heap here is the process memory region, unrelated to the priority-queue data structure.
